lessons.title: SaMD, IEC 62304 and what AI changes
lessons.summary: You will be able to tell when software is likely a medical device, explain the IEC 62304 lifecycle and safety classes, and list what extra work an AI model brings.
lessons.why: Software engineers are often surprised to learn that a feature they built is regulated as a medical device. Once it is, the way you plan, write, test, release and maintain it must follow a defined lifecycle, and every change needs evidence. If the software uses AI, regulators also expect you to show how the model was built, how well it performs, and how you will manage it as it changes. Knowing this early saves a project from rework or from shipping something that cannot legally be sold.

p: Software can be a medical device on its own, or it can be part of a hardware device. The International Medical Device Regulators Forum (IMDRF) defines software as a medical device (SaMD) as software intended to be used for one or more medical purposes that performs those purposes without being part of a hardware medical device. Firmware that runs an infusion pump is software in a medical device; an app that analyses heart rhythm data to flag a condition can be SaMD.
Whether software is a device depends on its intended use, meaning what the maker says it is for, not on the technology inside it. The same code can be a device in one product and not in another.

In the US, the starting point is the legal definition of a device and the FDA's guidance on device software functions. Some software functions are excluded from the device definition by law, such as many administrative and general wellness functions, and FDA guidance explains which. Clinical decision support software has its own FDA guidance that sets out when it is and is not a device. In the EU, the Medical Device Regulation (EU) 2017/745 applies, with a specific classification rule for software.

As an engineer you do not make this call alone. Your job is to describe clearly what the software does, who uses it and what decision it informs, so the regulatory team can decide. Watch for wording in requirements or marketing like 'diagnoses', 'detects', 'recommends a dose' or 'alerts the clinician', which often signals a device function.

IEC 62304 is the international standard for medical device software lifecycle processes. It assumes the maker already runs a quality management system and applies risk management under ISO 14971; it adds what is specific to software. Regulators widely recognise it.
list: Development process: plan, software requirements, architecture, detailed design, unit implementation and verification, integration and integration testing, system testing, release.
Maintenance process: how changes and fixes after release are planned, analysed and made.
Software risk management: how software can contribute to hazardous situations and how those risks are controlled, linked to the ISO 14971 file.
Configuration management: identifying every item and version, including third-party parts, and controlling changes to them.
Problem resolution: how bugs and anomalies are recorded, investigated and closed.
SOUP (software of unknown provenance): third-party or legacy software not developed under this process. You must state what you need from it, check its known issues, and control its version.

p: IEC 62304 sorts each software system into a safety class based on the worst harm its failure could contribute to, after considering risk controls outside the software. Class A: no injury or damage to health is possible. Class B: non-serious injury is possible. Class C: death or serious injury is possible.

The class decides how much process and documentation is required. Class A needs the least; class C asks for the most, including detailed design and more rigorous unit verification. Teams often split the architecture so that the parts that can cause serious harm are segregated, and only those parts carry the highest class, which keeps the rest of the system lighter to maintain.

sections.h: What changes when the software contains AI
p: IEC 62304 still applies to the software around the model, but a trained model brings questions that classic code does not. The FDA, Health Canada and the UK MHRA published ten guiding principles for good machine learning practice (GMLP), and the FDA has guidance on AI-enabled device software functions and on predetermined change control plans (PCCPs).
list: Data: training and test data must represent the intended patients and settings, and test data must be kept independent of training data.
Performance: report how well the model works on relevant subgroups and in conditions close to real use, not just one overall number.
Human and model together: show how the user will see and act on the output, and test the human with the model, not the model alone.
Monitoring: plan how to watch performance after release and catch drift when real data starts to differ from training data.

Planned change: a PCCP lets a maker describe in its marketing submission the model changes it plans, how they will be developed and validated, and how their impact will be assessed, so those changes can be made within the authorised plan.

Third-party models: a model you did not build, such as a hosted large language model, is close to what IEC 62304 calls SOUP. A common approach is to specify what you need from it, test it for your use, and pin and control its version.

example.title: Worked example: an AI early warning score in a hospital (example scenario)
p: A hospital group asks an engineering team to build software that reads vital signs from bedside monitors every 15 minutes and uses a machine learning model to flag patients at risk of rapid deterioration to the ward nurse. Walk through the questions the team asks before writing code.
The team ends up with a smaller first release, a clear class, and a plan for how the model can be updated. None of this was code, but all of it shaped the code.
list: Is it a device? It analyses physiological signals from a device to flag a time-critical condition for a clinician. The regulatory team reviews it against FDA's clinical decision support guidance and concludes it is very likely a device function.

Safety class: if the model misses a deteriorating patient, treatment could be delayed and serious injury is possible. There is no reliable external control, so the system would be class C. The team splits the design so the scoring and alerting part is segregated and carries class C, while the reporting dashboard is class A.
SOUP: the open source ML library and the database are listed as SOUP with versions, required behaviour and known issues reviewed.
Data: training and test data come from different hospitals and time periods, and performance is reported by age group, sex and ward type.
Human factors: nurses test the alert screen in simulated use, including what happens when they disagree with the score.
Change plan: the team drafts a PCCP describing planned retraining on new data, the test protocol each new model must pass, and how impact will be assessed.

practice.title: Classify three software features
practice.goal: Practise judging whether a feature is likely a device and which safety class it would carry.
steps: Read the FDA pages 'How to Determine if Your Product is a Medical Device' and 'Software as a Medical Device (SaMD)' linked below.
Write three short feature descriptions: one administrative (for example appointment booking), one wellness (for example step counting), one clinical (for example flagging irregular heart rhythm).
For each, write the intended use in one sentence and whether you think it is likely a device function, with your reason.
For any feature you think is a device, write the worst harm a failure could contribute to and the IEC 62304 class it would carry.
Ask Claude to argue the opposite view for each feature, then note what extra facts you would need from the regulatory team.
practice.done_when: You have a table of three features, each with intended use, device judgement with reason, and a safety class where relevant, plus a list of open questions.

pitfalls: Assuming software is not a device because it 'only gives advice'. Intended use and what decision it informs decide, not the form of the output.
Putting the whole system in class C because one part is. Segregate the high-risk parts so the rest can be maintained with a lighter process.
Using third-party libraries or hosted models without listing them as SOUP with pinned versions and known issues reviewed.
Reporting one overall accuracy figure for an AI model. Show performance on relevant subgroups and in conditions close to real use, and plan monitoring after release.

Ask the users to download and install it themselves

Segregate the alert module as class C

Whether a much larger model would score even higher
Whether the training data can be reused as test data

options: It replaces the need for a quality management system
It replaces ISO 14971 risk management for software
It applies only to software in safety class C
It builds on a QMS and ISO 14971

questions.q: A product manager writes 'the app recommends the insulin dose' in the requirements. What should the engineer do?
options: Nothing, since the wording of requirements does not matter
Remove the word 'recommends' so the app avoids regulation
Flag it to the regulatory team
Ship it as a general wellness app to keep things simple
questions.why: Words like 'recommends a dose' often signal a device function; regulatory decides, based on intended use.

Avoid recording which model version is in use in production
questions.why: A model you did not build is close to SOUP; specify, test and control its version.

Re-running the original unit tests from the first release
Raising the IEC 62304 safety class of the whole system
questions.why: Monitoring after release catches drift when real data starts to differ from training data.

lessons.title: Is this software a device, and which kind of software is it?
lessons.summary: You will be able to sort software in a device company into product, production and QMS, or non-device software, and describe a software function well enough for the regulatory team to qualify and classify it.
lessons.why: On a MedTech engagement you will meet many kinds of software: the app the patient uses, the test script on the production line, the complaint handling system, the analytics dashboard. They are governed by different rules. If you treat a production tool like a device you waste months; if you treat a device function like an internal tool, the product may be sold illegally. Getting the category right on day one decides which process, which evidence and which approvers your work needs.

sections.h: Three kinds of software in a device company
p: Start by asking what the software is for, not what it is built with. In a medical device company almost all software falls into one of three groups, and each group follows a different set of rules.

The line between the first two groups matters most for an FDE. A defect in product software can reach a patient directly. A defect in production or QMS software reaches the patient indirectly, by letting a bad unit ship or a complaint go unhandled. Both need evidence, but the evidence is different, and so are the people who approve it.
list: Product software: software that is a medical device on its own (software as a medical device, SaMD) or that runs inside or controls a device (software in a medical device). It goes through design controls, the IEC 62304 lifecycle and, where required, a premarket submission to a regulator.

Production and QMS software: software the manufacturer uses to make, test, release or control the quality of devices. Examples are a manufacturing execution system, an automated test station script, an electronic QMS, a complaint handling system or a label printing tool. It is not a device and is not submitted to a regulator. Under the US Quality Management System Regulation (21 CFR 820) and ISO 13485, it must be validated for its intended use, and FDA's computer software assurance guidance describes a risk-based way to do that.
Non-device software: software that does neither, such as a billing system, an appointment app or a marketing website. Normal good engineering applies, but no device rules.

sections.h: Intended use and indications for use
p: Whether product software is a device depends on its intended use: the purpose the maker states or shows for it. Regulators look at labeling, instructions, the website, sales material and even what sales staff say. Indications for use go one level deeper and name the disease or condition and the patients the product is meant for.

This is why the same code can be a device in one product and not in another. A step counter sold for fitness is usually not a device. The same algorithm sold to detect a heart condition is. If marketing changes the claim, the regulatory status can change without a single line of code changing.

In the US a device is defined in section 201(h) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. The 21st Century Cures Act then excluded several kinds of software functions from that definition, including administrative support, general wellness, electronic health records, functions that only transfer, store, convert or display data, and some clinical decision support. FDA's guidance on device software functions and mobile medical applications explains where these lines fall, and it also lists low-risk device functions for which FDA intends not to enforce its requirements.

Clinical decision support (CDS) software has its own guidance, which FDA revised in January 2026. In short, CDS falls outside the device definition only when it meets all of the criteria in the law: it does not analyse medical images or signals, it uses medical information about a patient, it supports a health care professional rather than replacing their judgement, and the professional can independently review the basis for the recommendation. Software that reads an ECG signal or a CT image fails the first test.

If a function is a device, FDA places it in class I, II or III by risk, which leads to a pathway such as 510(k), De Novo or premarket approval. A product with several functions is assessed function by function, using FDA's multiple function device products guidance.

In the EU the Medical Device Regulation (EU) 2017/745 (MDR) applies. The Medical Device Coordination Group guidance MDCG 2019-11, revised in June 2025, walks through qualification step by step: is it software, does it act on data for the benefit of individual patients, and does it have a medical purpose listed in the MDR definition?

Classification then uses Rule 11 in Annex VIII of the MDR. Software that provides information used to take diagnostic or therapeutic decisions is at least class IIa, rising to IIb or III when a wrong decision could cause serious deterioration of health or death. Software that monitors physiological processes is class IIa, or IIb when it monitors vital parameters where changes could mean immediate danger. Other software is class I. In practice many software devices end up class IIa or higher in the EU, which means a notified body must review them.

Qualification and classification are regulatory decisions, made by the manufacturer's regulatory team and recorded with a rationale. Your job is to give them a clear, honest description of each software function. A useful format is a function inventory: one row per function, with its inputs, what it does to them, its output, who sees the output, and what decision that person makes with it.

Flag wording that signals a device function, such as 'detects', 'diagnoses', 'predicts deterioration' or 'recommends a dose'. Ask again whenever the claims, users or inputs change, because the answer can change too.

example.title: Worked example: sorting the software in a remote monitoring program (example scenario)
p: A device maker runs a home blood pressure program. A team is asked to list all the software involved before planning a new release. Here is how they sort it, and what they hand to the regulatory team.

The team does not decide the final answers. They hand regulatory a function inventory with clear descriptions and open questions, and they now know which parts of their plan need the IEC 62304 process and which need software validation under the QMS.
list: Patient app shows readings from a cleared blood pressure cuff in a simple log: possibly an excluded display function or low risk; regulatory to confirm.
Patient app sends appointment reminders: administrative, likely non-device.

Nurse dashboard flags patients whose readings meet a risk score calculated by a model from several signals: analyses patient data to flag a condition, likely a device function. In the EU, Rule 11 would apply.
Firmware in the cuff: software in a medical device, already part of the cleared cuff.
Production line test script that checks each cuff's pressure sensor before release: production software, validated under the QMS, not submitted.
Complaint handling system that logs patient issues: QMS software, validated for its intended use.

practice.title: Build a software function inventory
practice.goal: Practise describing software functions so they can be qualified, and sorting product software from production and QMS software.
steps: Read FDA's page 'Step 1: Is the Software Function Intended for a Medical Purpose?' and skim the decision steps in MDCG 2019-11 rev.1, both linked below.
Pick a public description of a connected health product, such as a glucose monitor app or a sleep app, from its website.
In a spreadsheet, make one row per software function with columns: input, processing, output, user, decision informed, claim wording.
Add three rows for software the maker would use in production or quality, such as a test station, a complaint system and a label printer.
For each row mark product, production or QMS, or non-device, with a one-line reason and any device-signal words you found.
Ask Claude to challenge two of your calls, and write down which facts would settle each one.
practice.done_when: Your spreadsheet has at least eight rows, each with a category, a reason, and either a confident call or a named open question for the regulatory team.

pitfalls: Treating a production test script or complaint system as product software, and putting it through IEC 62304 and submission planning it does not need, instead of risk-based validation under the QMS.
Assuming that because an internal tool is not a device it needs no evidence at all. Production and QMS software still has to be validated for its intended use.
Judging device status from the code alone. Claims on the website and in sales material are part of intended use and can turn the same code into a device.
Assessing the product as one block. A product with several functions is assessed function by function, and one device function does not make every function a device.
Assuming the US and EU answers will match. Rule 11 in the EU often places software in a higher class than an engineer expects.

lessons.title: The IEC 62304 development process, step by step
lessons.summary: You will be able to name each IEC 62304 development activity, say what record it produces, and trace one requirement from risk control to released test evidence.
lessons.why: When you write code for a device, the code is only half the deliverable. The other half is the evidence that it was planned, specified, designed and tested in a controlled way, so a reviewer can trust it without reading every line. If you know what each activity must produce, you can build that evidence as you go instead of reconstructing it in a panic before release.

p: IEC 62304 describes what a manufacturer must do to develop product software: the software that is a device or runs inside one. It does not tell you which language, tools or method to use. It tells you which activities must happen and what each must produce, and it scales the work by safety class A, B or C.

It does not cover production or QMS software, such as a factory test script or a complaint system. That software is validated for its intended use under the QMS, using a risk-based approach like the one in FDA's computer software assurance guidance. Keep the two separate in your head and in your plans.

The development activities run in a logical order, from plan to release, but the standard allows you to repeat them in short cycles. What matters is that each output exists, is reviewed, and links to the others.

The software development plan says how the work will be done: the activities and deliverables, the standards, methods and tools, how traceability is kept between system requirements, software requirements, tests and risk controls, how configuration and changes are managed, and how verification will be done. It is a living document and must be updated as the project changes.
Software requirements state what the software must do. Good ones are specific and testable, and they include more than features.

Before design starts, the requirements themselves are checked. Each one should trace to a system requirement or risk control, be free of contradictions, be written so it can be tested, and be clear enough that two engineers would build the same thing. When the system requirements or the risk file change, the software requirements are re-checked and updated, which is why the plan says how traceability is kept.
list: Functions and capabilities, inputs and outputs, and interfaces with other systems.
Alarms, warnings and messages to the user.
Security requirements, such as authentication and protection of data.
Requirements that come from usability work and from data definitions.
Risk control measures that are implemented in software. These must be visible as requirements so they are tested.

p: The architecture breaks the software into software items and shows their interfaces, including interfaces to third-party software (SOUP). It is where you show segregation between items of different risk, and where you state what each SOUP item must do and what hardware and software it needs. Architecture is required for class B and C.

Each item is then broken into software units, the smallest pieces you verify. Class C also needs a documented detailed design for each unit and its interfaces, detailed enough to implement correctly. For class B and C, each unit must be verified against acceptance criteria you define, using reviews, static analysis or unit tests. Class C adds extra criteria, such as correct event sequence, data and control flow, fault handling and initialisation.

Integration testing checks that the units and items work together as the architecture says, including SOUP. System testing checks the whole software system against every software requirement. Each test record names the version tested, who tested it, the result, and the expected and actual outcome. Any failure goes into the problem resolution process, and after a fix you run regression tests to show nothing else broke.

Release is a deliberate step, not the last merge. Before release you confirm that verification is complete, list the known residual anomalies, the bugs you are not fixing, and evaluate each one to show it does not create unacceptable risk. You document the exact version released and how it was built, so it can be rebuilt, and you archive the software and its records.

Nothing in IEC 62304 forces a waterfall model. Many teams run sprints and map them to the standard. The AAMI technical report TIR45 gives guidance on using agile methods for medical device software. The practical approach is to make the standard's outputs part of your normal work.

Put requirements and risk controls in the same tool as your backlog, link each test to its requirement, and include document updates in the definition of done. Use continuous integration to run unit and integration tests on every change and keep the results. Hold a formal system test and release review for each release candidate, because a sprint demo is not release evidence.

Watch for one common trap: the backlog tool keeps changing, so the evidence must be frozen. At each release, export or baseline the requirements, tests and trace links as they stood for that version, so a reviewer months later sees exactly what was true at release, not what the tool shows today.

example.title: Worked example: tracing one requirement end to end (example scenario)
p: A class B glucose diary app lets patients type in meter readings, and the risk file notes that a typing error, such as 55 entered as 555, could lead the patient to a wrong action. The team traces the risk control through every activity. The identifiers and limits below are illustrative.
At release, a reviewer can start at the hazard and follow links to passing evidence, or start at a test and see why it exists. That two-way link is what traceability means in practice.
list: Risk file: hazardous situation 'implausible reading accepted' with risk control RC-07 'reject values outside the meter's measuring range and ask the user to re-enter'.
Software requirement SRS-014: the app shall reject a glucose value outside the configured range and show message M-12. It links to RC-07.
Architecture: the input validation item owns this rule; the range is read from a controlled configuration file.
Unit verification: unit tests cover the lower and upper limits, one below, one above, empty input and non-numeric input. They run in continuous integration.
System test TC-031: a tester enters out-of-range values on a release build and checks message M-12. The record shows build number, tester, date and result.
Release: the traceability report shows RC-07 to SRS-014 to TC-031 all passing, and one cosmetic anomaly in the message text is listed and evaluated as no safety impact.

practice.title: Write a mini plan and traceability matrix
practice.goal: Produce the core development records for a small feature and see how they link.
steps: Pick a small device feature, such as a medication reminder that warns when two doses are logged too close together.
Write a one-page development plan: activities, tools, how you will trace requirements to tests, and how you will handle changes and bugs.
Write five software requirements, including at least one alarm and one risk control, each specific and testable.
In a spreadsheet, build a traceability matrix with columns: risk control, requirement, architecture item, unit test, system test, result.
Write two system test cases with steps, expected result and a blank for actual result and tester.

lessons.title: Safety classes, SOUP and architecture in practice
lessons.summary: You will be able to justify a software safety class from the risk file, design segregation that holds up in review, and keep SOUP and SBOM records that support both safety and cybersecurity.
lessons.why: The safety class decides how much work every later step needs, and SOUP is in almost every modern product: open source libraries, operating systems, databases, cloud SDKs and models. FDEs are often the ones adding a library or a model to a device codebase. Knowing how a class is argued, how segregation is shown and what a SOUP record needs keeps a quick integration from turning into a release blocker.

sections.h: Assigning and documenting the safety class
p: The class comes from the risk file, not from a gut feeling. Start with the hazardous situations in the ISO 14971 risk analysis that software could contribute to. For each one, assume the software fails: software failures are systematic, so you cannot argue they are unlikely the way you might for a worn part. Then ask what harm could follow, after considering risk control measures outside the software system, such as a hardware limit, an independent alarm or a clinical check.

If no hazardous situation can arise, or none leads to unacceptable risk after external controls, the system is class A. If the worst outcome is non-serious injury, class B. If death or serious injury is possible, class C. Write down the reasoning, the hazards considered and the external controls relied on. Software items inherit the class of the system unless you document why a lower class is justified for a segregated item.

Segregation lets you keep the class C work small. The idea is simple: if a lower-class item fails, it must not be able to make the higher-class item fail. Folders, namespaces or separate Git repositories are not segregation on their own, because the code still shares memory, threads and data.
Credible segregation usually rests on runtime separation and controlled interfaces, and you must explain in the architecture why it is effective.
list: Separate processes or processors with operating system memory protection.
Interfaces that pass data one way, with the receiving item checking every value it gets.
Independent watchdogs or monitors that can stop or override the higher-risk function.
Separate deployment, so a crash or update of the low-risk item cannot stop the high-risk one.

p: SOUP, software of unknown provenance, is software you did not develop under your IEC 62304 process: open source libraries, commercial components, operating systems, and legacy code. You do not have to prove how it was built, but you must control how you use it. FDA's guidance on off-the-shelf software use in medical devices covers the same ground from the regulator's side.
For each SOUP item, record:

The same thinking applies to things that are not classic libraries. A pre-trained model you download, a cloud service your software calls, or a hosted language model all behave like SOUP: you did not build them under your process, they can change, and they can fail in ways you must anticipate. Treat their version or model identifier as a controlled item, state what you need from them, and test that on your own data.
list: Its name, supplier and exact version, pinned so it cannot change silently.
The functional and performance requirements your software needs from it, for class B and C.
The hardware and software it needs to run correctly.
A review of its published known anomalies, such as the issue tracker or release notes, judging whether any could contribute to a hazardous situation.
How you will keep watching for new anomalies and vulnerabilities after release.

p: A software bill of materials (SBOM) is a machine-readable list of every software component in the product, with versions, suppliers and dependency relationships, including the dependencies of your dependencies. Common formats are SPDX and CycloneDX, and many build tools can generate them.

The SOUP list and the SBOM overlap but serve different purposes. The SOUP list is safety documentation: what you need from each item and whether its known bugs matter. The SBOM is a complete inventory used mainly to find which products are affected when a new vulnerability is published. In the US, section 524B of the FD&C Act requires manufacturers of cyber devices to provide an SBOM covering commercial, open source and off-the-shelf components in their premarket submission. Generate the SBOM from the build, not by hand, so it matches what actually ships.

sections.h: Linking software to the ISO 14971 file
p: Software risk management in IEC 62304 is not a separate risk process; it feeds the device's ISO 14971 risk file. Each software item that can contribute to a hazardous situation is listed with the possible causes, such as a wrong calculation, a frozen screen, corrupted data or a SOUP failure. Each risk control in software becomes a requirement, is verified, and its verification is traced back in the risk file.
When software changes, check the risk file again: a new feature can add a cause, and a SOUP update can remove or add one. If the file and the code drift apart, the class argument no longer holds.

example.title: Worked example: how an external control changes the class (example scenario)
p: A team builds software that sets the delivery rate on an infusion device. A rate far above the prescription could cause serious injury. They work through the class argument twice, once with and once without a hardware control.
The point is not to aim for a lower class. It is to state honestly what protects the patient and to put the heavier process where the risk really is.
list: Without external control: if the software sets a wrong rate, nothing stops it. Serious injury is possible, so the rate control software is class C.

With an independent hardware flow limiter, built and verified outside the software, that caps the rate at a safe maximum: the team checks whether harm is still possible at rates below the cap. The clinical team says a rate just under the cap could still harm some patients, so the item stays class C.
The reporting screen that shows past infusions cannot change the rate and runs in a separate process. With that segregation documented, it is class A.
The team lists the real-time operating system and the database as SOUP, pins versions, reviews their published issue lists and records which issues were judged not relevant and why.
The SBOM is generated by the build pipeline for each release and stored with the release records.

practice.title: Build a SOUP list from a real project
practice.goal: See how many third-party components a small project really has and what a SOUP record needs.
steps: Create a Python virtual environment and install two common packages, for example requests and pandas, with pip.
Run 'python -m pip list --format=json' and save the output. Note how many packages you have compared with the two you asked for.
In a spreadsheet, make a SOUP table for five of the packages: name, version, supplier or project, what your software needs from it, and what it needs to run.
For each of the five, search osv.dev for known vulnerabilities in that version and read the project's recent issues or release notes.
Write one line per package on whether any known issue could matter for a device that displays lab results, and what you would do about it.
practice.done_when: You have a five-row SOUP table with pinned versions, stated requirements, a known-anomaly review date and a reasoned decision for each row.

pitfalls: Calling separate folders or repositories 'segregation' when the items share one process and can corrupt each other's memory or data.
Lowering the class by arguing that software failure is unlikely. IEC 62304 asks you to assume the software fails and rely only on controls outside it.
Listing only direct dependencies as SOUP and missing the libraries they pull in, which is where many vulnerabilities sit.
Writing the SBOM by hand once and never regenerating it, so it no longer matches the software that ships.
Letting the risk file and the code drift apart, so the safety class argument rests on an architecture that no longer exists.

lessons.title: Keeping released device software safe and secure
lessons.summary: You will be able to take a field problem or a new vulnerability through change analysis, a controlled fix and release, and explain what cybersecurity evidence regulators expect before and after market.
lessons.why: Most of a device's software life happens after its first release. Bugs are reported, SOUP gets new versions, and vulnerabilities are published in components you ship. Each of these needs a controlled response: a quick hotfix pushed without analysis can create a new hazard or a regulatory problem, and a known vulnerability left alone can put patients and hospitals at risk. FDEs often work on exactly these changes.

p: IEC 62304 asks for a software maintenance plan: how feedback is collected after release, how it is evaluated, which items become problem reports, and how changes are made and released. Feedback includes complaints, service reports, internal testing, SOUP updates and security advisories.

Every proposed change is analysed before work starts. Does it affect safety: could it add a hazard cause, change a risk control or touch a higher-class item? Does it affect regulatory status: in the US, FDA's guidance on deciding when to submit a 510(k) for a software change helps answer whether a new submission is needed, and in the EU a significant change may need notified body review. Only then is the change made, using the same development process, with regression testing sized to what the change could affect.

A problem report records what was seen, which version, how severe it is and whether it affects safety. The team investigates the cause, decides whether and how to fix it, and tracks the report to closure, including verification that the fix works and did not break anything else.

Problem resolution in software links to the wider QMS. A software problem found through a complaint is also a complaint record, and a pattern of similar problems may need a corrective and preventive action (CAPA). That is why the standard asks you to analyse problem reports for trends, not just close them one by one. Ten small reports about the same screen can point to one design flaw.
Configuration management means you can always say exactly what is in a given release and rebuild it. Treat these as configuration items, each with an identifier and version:

Changes to any configuration item go through the same control: a change request, analysis, approval, and a record of what changed and why. In practice most of this lives in Git, the issue tracker and the build pipeline. The discipline is that nothing reaches a release build except through that route, and that release tags, SBOMs and test results are kept together so the history can be read back years later.
list: Source code, build scripts and the build toolchain versions.
Every SOUP item, pinned, and the generated SBOM.
Configuration files and parameters that change behaviour, such as alarm limits.
Trained models, their weights and the data versions used to train and test them.
Requirements, design, test and risk records for that release.
A record of which version is installed where, so you know who is affected by a problem.

p: Security is part of device safety: an attacker who can change a dose or stop an alarm creates a hazard. FDA's guidance on cybersecurity in medical devices sets out quality management system considerations and the content of premarket submissions. It expects a secure product development framework, threat modeling, a cybersecurity risk assessment, an SBOM, security architecture views, security testing such as penetration testing, labeling that tells users how to operate the device securely, and a plan for managing vulnerabilities after release.

Since 2023, section 524B of the FD&C Act has required manufacturers of cyber devices, which include software and can connect to the internet, to submit a plan to monitor and address postmarket vulnerabilities, to have processes that give reasonable assurance the device is cybersecure, and to provide an SBOM. In the EU, the MDR's general safety and performance requirements cover IT security, and MDCG 2019-16 gives guidance on cybersecurity for medical devices. IEC 81001-5-1 is the standard that adds security activities to the health software lifecycle.

Threat modeling is the step engineers can start on today. Draw the system with its data flows and trust boundaries, such as the device, the phone app, the cloud and the hospital network, then ask at each boundary how data could be read, changed, faked or blocked. Each credible threat goes into the security risk assessment, and the controls become requirements that are tested like any other.

When a vulnerability is published in a component you ship, you triage it. Is the vulnerable version in any product, according to the SBOM? Is the vulnerable function reachable in your use? What could an attacker do, and could that lead to patient harm? FDA's postmarket cybersecurity guidance frames the outcome as controlled or uncontrolled risk of patient harm, and expects faster action and communication when the risk is uncontrolled.

The patch itself is a change. It goes through change analysis, the development process and regression testing, because a new SOUP version can change behaviour your requirements depend on. Then you tell users and hospitals what changed and what they must do, through a coordinated vulnerability disclosure process. Production and QMS software gets patched too, but under the QMS change control and validation rules, not the device release process.

example.title: Worked example: a vulnerability in a connected device gateway (example scenario)
p: A hospital gateway sends readings from bedside devices to a cloud dashboard. A security advisory is published for the version of an open source web server library used in the gateway. Here is how the team works through it.
The team spent most of the effort on analysis and evidence, not on the code change itself. That is normal for released device software.
list: The SBOM shows the vulnerable version in gateway releases 3.1 and 3.2, installed at sites listed in the configuration records.
The team checks reachability: the vulnerable feature is used by the gateway's admin page, which is reachable on the hospital network.

Impact: an attacker could stop the gateway, so readings would stop reaching the dashboard. The bedside devices keep alarming locally, so the team, with the risk manager, rates the patient harm risk as controlled, while still planning a fix.
Change analysis: upgrading the library is a SOUP change in a class B item. Regulatory reviews it against the 510(k) software change guidance and records why no new submission is needed.
The upgrade is built, the SOUP record and SBOM are updated, and the regression suite plus targeted security tests run on release 3.3.
A customer notice explains the issue, the fix, and a temporary step of restricting admin page access until sites update.

practice.goal: Practise the reasoning behind a vulnerability triage record for device software.
steps: Search osv.dev or the NIST NVD for a published vulnerability in a widely used open source library, such as a JSON parser or web framework.
Read the advisory and write down the affected versions, the vulnerable function and what an attacker could do.
Imagine the library is SOUP in a class B infusion pump companion app that shows pump status to nurses. Write whether the function is likely reachable, and why.
Write a one-paragraph harm assessment and whether you would call the risk of patient harm controlled or uncontrolled, with your reason.
List the records you would update: problem report, SOUP entry, SBOM, risk file, release notes, customer notice.

pitfalls: Pushing a hotfix straight to the field without change analysis, so a new hazard or a missed regulatory submission slips through.
Closing problem reports one at a time without trending them, and missing a design flaw that shows up as many small complaints.
Treating cybersecurity as an IT topic separate from safety, when an attack that changes device behaviour is a hazard in the risk file.
Upgrading a SOUP version to fix a vulnerability without regression testing, even though the new version can change behaviour.
Not knowing which software version is installed at which site, so you cannot tell who is affected by a problem.

lessons.title: Building and evidencing AI-enabled device software
lessons.summary: You will be able to plan the data, evaluation, transparency and change control work an AI-enabled device function needs, and explain where generative AI and the EU AI Act add to it.
lessons.why: FDEs are often asked to add a model to a clinical workflow because the prototype looked impressive. In a device, a good demo is not evidence. Regulators want to know where the data came from, whether the test was fair, who the model fails for, how the user sees its limits, and how you will control it when it changes. Building that in from the start is much cheaper than retrofitting it before a submission.

p: The FDA, Health Canada and the UK MHRA published ten guiding principles for good machine learning practice (GMLP). They are short and worth reading in full. In summary they ask for: people with clinical, data and engineering expertise across the whole lifecycle; good software engineering and security practice; data that represents the intended patients; training data kept independent of test data; reference standards chosen with the best available methods; a model design suited to the data and the intended use; a focus on how the human and the model perform together; testing in clinically relevant conditions; clear, essential information for users; and monitoring of deployed models with managed retraining.
None of this replaces IEC 62304 or ISO 14971. The code around the model still follows the software lifecycle, and the model's failure modes go into the risk file.
Most AI device problems start in the data. Plan and record each of these before training:
list: Sourcing: which sites, devices, time periods and patient groups the data comes from, and whether that matches the intended use.
Reference standard: how the 'truth' label was set, by whom, with what instructions, and how disagreements were resolved.
Independence: the test set must not share patients, and ideally not sites, with the training set. Splitting by image instead of by patient leaks information and inflates results.
Lineage: dataset versions, inclusion and exclusion rules, and any cleaning steps, kept as configuration items.
Privacy and permissions: the legal basis for using the data, handled with the data owner.

p: Define acceptance criteria before you test, tied to clinical need: for example a minimum sensitivity so few real cases are missed, and a minimum specificity so clinicians are not flooded with false alarms. Report confidence intervals, not just point values, because a small test set gives an uncertain answer.

Then break results down by subgroups that matter for the intended use, such as age, sex, ethnicity or skin type, device model and site. A model can look strong overall and fail a group that was small in the data. Where the user decides with the model's help, test the user and model together in realistic conditions, because that is the performance patients actually get.

FDA, Health Canada and the MHRA also published guiding principles on transparency for machine learning-enabled devices. The user should know what the device is for, what inputs it expects, how well it performed and for whom, its known limits, and how its output should be used in their decision. Put this where it is used: in the interface and labeling, not only in a technical file.

Design the screen so the output cannot be misread. Show when an input is outside what the model was tested on, and make it clear the output supports a decision rather than making it, if that is the intended use. Human factors testing should include cases where the model is wrong.

Models drift when real data moves away from training data: a new scanner, a new patient mix, a new clinical practice. Plan monitoring before release: which signals you watch, how you get ground truth in the field, and what triggers investigation.

In the US, a predetermined change control plan (PCCP) is reviewed as part of the marketing submission. It has three parts: a description of the planned modifications, a modification protocol for how each will be developed, validated and implemented, and an impact assessment. Changes made within an authorised PCCP do not need a new submission each time; changes outside it follow the normal rules. FDA also has draft guidance, issued January 2025, on lifecycle management and marketing submissions for AI-enabled device software functions.

sections.h: Generative AI and the EU AI Act
p: Generative models bring extra problems: the same input can give different outputs, the model can state false things fluently, and a hosted model can change when the vendor updates it. Treat a third-party model like SOUP: pin the model version where the vendor allows it, treat prompts and retrieval settings as configuration items, build a fixed evaluation set for your intended use, and re-run it on every change. If the vendor cannot pin versions, that is a risk to raise early.

In the EU, the AI Act, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, treats an AI system as high-risk when it is a medical device, or a safety component of one, that needs notified body conformity assessment under the MDR or IVDR. High-risk systems carry AI Act duties on risk management, data governance, technical documentation, logging, transparency, human oversight, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity. MDCG 2025-6 explains how these fit alongside the MDR. Check the official text for the dates that apply to device makers.

example.title: Worked example: subgroup results for a skin lesion triage model (example scenario)
p: A team builds a model that flags skin lesion photos for urgent dermatology review. Overall sensitivity looks acceptable. Before accepting it, they break the test results down by skin type. The counts below are illustrative, not from a real study.

The code prints sensitivity 0.88, 0.80 and 0.70. The darkest skin type group has the lowest sensitivity and also the fewest cases, so its estimate is the least certain. The team does not average this away. They record it as a finding, collect more data from that group, set a subgroup acceptance criterion, and plan to state the limit in labeling if it remains.

code.text:
# Illustrative counts per subgroup: tp, fn, tn, fp
groups = {
    "Skin type I-II": {"tp": 88, "fn": 12, "tn": 270, "fp": 30},
    "Skin type III-IV": {"tp": 80, "fn": 20, "tn": 250, "fp": 50},
    "Skin type V-VI": {"tp": 21, "fn": 9, "tn": 60, "fp": 10},
}
for name, c in groups.items():
    sens = c["tp"] / (c["tp"] + c["fn"])
    spec = c["tn"] / (c["tn"] + c["fp"])
    n = sum(c.values())
    print(f"{name}: n={n} sensitivity={sens:.2f} specificity={spec:.2f}")

practice.title: Draft an evaluation plan for an AI device function
practice.goal: Turn GMLP principles into a concrete, checkable evaluation plan.
steps: Read FDA's GMLP guiding principles page and the transparency guiding principles page, both linked below.
Pick an AI function, such as flagging possible fractures on wrist X-rays for a radiologist.
Write the intended use, users and decision in three sentences.
List data sources, how labels are set, how you will split by patient and site, and three subgroups you will report.

Write three planned changes you might want later and, for each, one test it must pass before release.

Reporting one overall metric and hiding a subgroup where the model performs poorly.
Testing the model alone when the real use is a clinician deciding with its help, so the evaluated performance is not the one patients get.
Calling a hosted language model through an alias that the vendor can repoint to a new model, with no version pinning and no re-run of the evaluation set.

lessons.title: Software documentation for submissions and release readiness
lessons.summary: You will be able to choose the FDA documentation level with a rationale, list the software documents a submission needs in the US and the EU, and assemble a release-readiness pack that stays current.
lessons.why: A submission is where all the engineering evidence is judged at once. Missing or inconsistent software documents are a common reason for review questions and delays. FDEs rarely write the whole submission, but they are often asked to produce the software parts: architecture, test summaries, version history and the list of unresolved anomalies. If those are generated from the real project records, the submission becomes an export, not a rewrite.

p: FDA's guidance 'Content of Premarket Submissions for Device Software Functions' sets out the software documentation for 510(k), De Novo and PMA submissions. It applies to product software: software functions that meet the device definition. Production and QMS software is not part of the submission; it is validated and kept under the QMS, where an inspector may review it.
The guidance lists these documentation elements:
list: Documentation level evaluation: the level and the rationale for it.
Software description: features, functions, inputs, outputs and hardware platforms.
Risk management file: plan, assessment showing risks are mitigated, and report.
Software requirements specification (SRS), with enough detail to follow traceability.
System and software architecture design: modules, layers, interfaces and data flows, including how users and external systems connect.
Software design specification (SDS), submitted for the Enhanced level.
Software development, configuration management and maintenance practices, as summaries or a declaration of conformity to the FDA-recognised version of IEC 62304.
Software testing as part of verification and validation.
Software version history: tested versions, dates and what changed.
Unresolved software anomalies, each with an evaluation of its impact on safety and effectiveness.

p: There are two levels, Basic and Enhanced. Enhanced applies when a failure or flaw of any device software function could present a hazardous situation with a probable risk of death or serious injury to a patient, user or others. The guidance says to assess this before risk control measures are applied, and to include risks from foreseeable misuse and from weak cybersecurity. Everything else is Basic.

Note the contrast with IEC 62304 safety classes, which consider risk controls outside the software. Because the FDA level is judged before risk controls, a device can be IEC 62304 class B and still need Enhanced documentation. The level covers the device as a whole, not each function. Write the rationale with references to the risk file, so the reviewer can follow it.

The documentation level is about how much evidence FDA wants to see, not about how much engineering you do. A Basic device still needs a full design history file and proper testing; the difference is mainly what goes into the submission and what stays available on request. Deciding the level early lets the team plan which test protocols and design records must be review-ready.

In the EU, MDR Annexes II and III describe the technical documentation and post-market surveillance documentation. There is no separate software dossier: software evidence sits inside the device's technical documentation. For software this usually means the device description and intended purpose, the design and manufacturing information including architecture, the general safety and performance requirements checklist with the software and IT security requirements in Annex I, the risk management file, software verification and validation, and the clinical evaluation. MDCG 2020-1 gives guidance on clinical evaluation of medical device software.

For class IIa and above, a notified body reviews this documentation. Many teams keep one core set of software records and map it to both the FDA elements and the EU structure, rather than writing two versions.

Reviewers read the software documents together, so consistency matters as much as completeness. The software description, architecture, requirements and tests should use the same names for the same items, and the version tested should be the version described. A requirement that appears in the SRS but has no test, or a risk control in the risk file with no requirement, is an easy question for a reviewer to ask.

Make the evidence easy to follow. Keep the traceability from hazard to risk control to requirement to test visible, explain how regression testing was scoped for a modified device, and highlight the software changes that affect safety and effectiveness since the last cleared version. For each unresolved anomaly, say what the user would see, why it is acceptable, and any workaround. Clear, short documents with good cross-references get fewer questions than long ones that hide the key facts.

sections.h: Keeping documentation in step with releases
p: Documents go stale when they are written by hand at the end. The sustainable approach is to keep requirements, risk controls, tests and anomalies in tools, link them, and generate the submission documents and reports from those links for each release. Treat the generated documents as part of the release baseline, versioned with the software.

A release-readiness pack is a useful habit even when no submission is due. It answers, for one version: what changed, what was tested, what passed, what is still open and why that is acceptable. When a submission or audit comes, most of the work is already done.

example.title: Worked example: a release-readiness pack for version 2.3 (example scenario)
p: A class B remote monitoring app is preparing version 2.3, which adds a new alert type. Regulatory says the change needs a new 510(k). The team builds the pack from its tools, and the documentation level rationale concludes Basic, because no software failure could present a probable risk of death or serious injury even before risk controls. Regulatory reviews and signs that rationale.

Because each item came from linked records, the team could answer the reviewer's later question about one anomaly within the hour, by following its links to the risk file and the test that showed the workaround is effective.
list: Version history: 2.3 build number, date, and a short list of changes since the last cleared version, with the new alert highlighted.
Traceability report: each new or changed requirement linked to its risk control, architecture item and passing system test.
Test summary: unit and integration testing described, system test protocol and report attached, regression scope explained.
SOUP list and SBOM generated from the 2.3 build, with known anomaly review dates.
Unresolved anomalies: four items, each with its symptom, root cause if known, workaround and an evaluation of impact on safety and effectiveness.
Cybersecurity documents updated for the new alert's data flow.

practice.goal: Practise building submission-style software evidence from linked records.

pitfalls: Choosing the documentation level after counting risk controls, which can lead to Basic documentation when Enhanced is needed.
Listing unresolved anomalies without an evaluation of each one's impact on safety and effectiveness.
Writing submission documents by hand from memory, so the architecture or test summary no longer matches the version being submitted.
Preparing separate, inconsistent software documents for the FDA and the EU instead of mapping one core set of records to both.
Adding production or QMS software validation records to the device submission, where they do not belong, while missing the product software elements.
